results.result: Mice fed a high-fat high-sucrose diet (HFHSD) develop glucose intolerance and tissue-specific insulin resistance with distinct temporal patterns. Glucose intolerance appears by day 1 and plateaus by day 14. Adipose tissue insulin resistance is observed by day 5 and maintained through day 42, while skeletal muscle shows delayed onset with maximal insulin resistance by day 14.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C6 are well-supported by glucose tolerance test data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B) and tissue-specific 3H-2-DOG uptake measurements (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-D). The temporal progression is clearly documented with appropriate statistical comparisons. The delayed muscle response is consistent with cited prior work (Turner et al., 2013).

results.result: In vitro insulin resistance models are characterized by impaired HA-GLUT4 translocation to the plasma membrane and reduced insulin-mediated 2-deoxyglucose uptake.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8 are supported by data in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E showing reduced HA-GLUT4 translocation and 2DOG uptake in 3T3-L1 adipocytes treated with chronic insulin, dexamethasone, or TNFα. These are standard, well-validated measures of insulin sensitivity in adipocytes.

results.result: Proteomic analysis of insulin-resistant adipose tissue and 3T3-L1 adipocytes quantified 2981 and 3494 proteins respectively, with 98 proteins altered at both 5 and 14 day HFHSD time points, 491 proteins altered in ≥2 in vitro models, and 19 proteins common to both in vivo and in vitro analyses, including LRPAP1.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C14 are supported by proteomic data presented in Figure 1C-D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, and Supplementary files. The numbers of proteins quantified and overlapping between conditions are clearly documented. The identification of LRPAP1 is supported by citation to Jedrychowski et al., 2010 regarding its role in GLUT4 trafficking.

results.result: Gene set enrichment analysis identified 13 pathways altered at both 5 and 14 day HFHSD time points in adipose tissue, with high overlap in altered pathways across in vitro models, and 10 pathways overlapping between all models.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C18 are supported by gene set enrichment analysis data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G and Supplementary file 1-tab E. The pathway analysis methodology is appropriate and the overlap between models is clearly documented.

results.result: Parallel analysis of gene expression and proteomics revealed minimal overlap between regulated transcripts and proteins across all insulin resistance models, with only 12 of 98 proteins altered at both HFHSD time points also showing mRNA changes, emphasizing the importance of proteomic analysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C22 are supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H-M and Supplementary file 2. The lack of concordance between mRNA and protein is clearly demonstrated. However, C22 is an inference about the importance of proteomics rather than a direct finding. The conclusion is reasonable but represents interpretation.

results.result: Integrated pathway analysis identified 13 KEGG pathways highly altered (z-score >4) in both in vivo and in vitro models, with oxidative phosphorylation most highly altered, followed by TCA cycle, branched chain amino acid metabolism, proteasome, ribosome, spliceosome, N-glycan biosynthesis, and terpenoid backbone biosynthesis/mevalonate pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C25 are supported by pathway analysis data in Figure 1E and Supplementary file 3-tab B. The combined z-score approach for integrating across models is appropriate and the pathways identified are clearly ranked.

results.result: Proteomic analysis of adipose tissue from 22 obese subjects quantified 4481 proteins and identified 299 proteins and 26 pathways positively correlated with insulin sensitivity, and 142 proteins and 2 pathways (ribosome, spliceosome) negatively correlated with insulin sensitivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C30 are supported by proteomic data in Supplementary file 3-tabs A-B. The correlation threshold (r = <−0.423 or >0.423) is stated but the rationale for this specific cutoff is not provided. The sample size of 22 subjects is modest for correlation analysis but appears adequate given the effect sizes.

results.result: The PPAR signalling pathway, a known regulator of adipose insulin sensitivity, was positively associated with insulin sensitivity in the human cohort analysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C32 are supported by pathway correlation data and citation to Sugii et al., 2009. This serves as a positive control validating the analysis pipeline, as PPAR signaling is an established regulator of adipose insulin sensitivity.

results.result: Of 13 pathways of interest from integrated proteomic analysis, only 5 were positively associated with insulin sensitivity in human adipose tissue: spliceosome, central carbon metabolism, amino acid metabolism including branched chain amino acid synthesis/degradation, and the terpenoid backbone biosynthesis/mevalonate pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C34 are supported by data in Figure 1F and Supplementary file 3-tab B. The filtering from 13 to 5 pathways based on human data is clearly documented. C34 is established biochemical knowledge about the mevalonate pathway.

results.result: Branched chain amino acid metabolism and spliceosome function have been implicated in adipocyte or whole body insulin sensitivity, providing support for the analysis pipeline.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C36 are supported by citations to Newgard et al., 2009 and Vernia et al., 2016. These serve as additional validation that the pathway analysis is identifying biologically relevant processes.

results.result: COQ7 and COQ9 protein levels were lower in insulin-resistant adipose tissue from humans and mice, while ADCK3/COQ8 was dysregulated at protein and mRNA levels in vitro, pointing toward convergence upon dysregulated CoQ biosynthesis in insulin resistance.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C39 are supported by proteomic data in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1. C40 is an inference about convergence that is reasonable given the consistent changes across models. The data clearly show alterations in CoQ biosynthesis pathway components.

results.result: Whole-cell CoQ concentrations were decreased in in vitro models but not in insulin-resistant adipose tissue. However, subcellular fractionation revealed selective depletion of CoQ in mitochondria across all models, which was not due to changes in mitochondrial content.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C44 are supported by CoQ measurement data in Figure 3A-D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-J, and Supplementary file 2-tabs A-D. The subcellular fractionation approach is appropriate and the normalization to citrate synthase activity and OXPHOS subunit abundance controls for mitochondrial content. This is a key finding showing compartment-specific CoQ depletion.

results.result: In obese humans, adipose tissue mitochondrial CoQ10 was positively correlated with insulin-induced suppression of NEFAs and whole-body insulin sensitivity (GIR), and with expression of CoQ biosynthesis pathway proteins (r=+0.52), independent of age or BMI, indicating that decreased mitochondrial CoQ is an obesity-independent feature of adipocyte insulin resistance.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C50 are supported by data in Figure 3E-F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1K-L, Table 1, and Supplementary file 3-tab B. The correlations are statistically significant and the stratification analysis in Table 1 shows no effect of age or BMI. C48 and C50 are inferences that are reasonable given the correlation data. The sample size (n=22) is modest but adequate for the observed effect sizes.

results.result: CoQ biosynthesis rates were lower in cells treated with dexamethasone or TNFα but elevated in chronic insulin-treated cells. Dexamethasone and TNFα likely lower mitochondrial CoQ via reduced biosynthesis, though increased CoQ in microsomal and PM fractions suggests additional dysregulation of CoQ trafficking. Additional pathways likely contribute to dysregulated mitochondrial CoQ homeostasis in chronic insulin-treated adipocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C52 are supported by CoQ biosynthesis rate data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1Q. C53-C56 are inferences about mechanisms that are reasonable given the data but represent speculation. The paradox of elevated biosynthesis but lower mitochondrial CoQ in chronic insulin model is acknowledged and suggests additional regulatory mechanisms.

results.result: Mitochondrial CoQ was decreased at 14 and 42 day HFHSD feeding in muscle, correlating with emergence of insulin resistance, while liver mitochondrial CoQ was unchanged. Changes in cholesterol content were inconsistent with a causal role in insulin resistance across tissues, suggesting decreased mitochondrial CoQ may be involved at an early stage in insulin resistance development in muscle and adipose tissue.
results.evaluation: Claims C57, C60-C61 are supported by CoQ and cholesterol measurement data in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1M-W. C58 and C62 are inferences about temporal correlation and causality that are reasonable but speculative. The tissue-specific differences (muscle and adipose affected, liver not) are clearly documented.

results.result: Addition of CoQ9 increased mitochondrial CoQ9 in insulin-resistant cells and both CoQ9 and CoQ10 improved insulin-stimulated HA-GLUT4 translocation and 2DOG uptake in all cell models. Dexamethasone or TNFα treatment enhanced basal lipolysis and insulin-regulated inhibition of lipolysis was defective in all models, but CoQ9 provision increased suppression of lipolysis by insulin in in vitro models.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C68 are supported by data in Figure 4A-C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-E. The improvement in insulin sensitivity with CoQ supplementation is clearly demonstrated across multiple measures (GLUT4 translocation, 2DOG uptake, lipolysis). The effect on lipolysis in the TNF model was not significant (p=0.11), which is appropriately noted.

results.result: CoQ10 administration improved whole-body glucose tolerance in mice fed a HFHSD for 5 or 14 days without altering insulin secretion, accompanied by increased suppression of NEFAs and 2DOG clearance into adipose depots and quadriceps during GTT. CoQ10 also increased insulin responsiveness during ITT as measured by blood glucose excursion and 2DOG uptake into fat pads and muscle.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C74 are supported by data in Figure 4D-K and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F-L. The in vivo effects of CoQ10 on glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity are clearly demonstrated. Some effects approached but did not reach significance (inguinal adipose p=0.06, quadriceps p=0.08), which is appropriately noted. The lack of effect on insulin secretion rules out beta-cell effects.

results.result: Administration of increasing doses of CoQ10 to HFHSD-fed mice for 14 days dose-dependently increased CoQ10 in mitochondria from epididymal adipose tissue, improved glucose tolerance, and improved insulin-stimulated 2DOG uptake in ex vivo adipose tissue explants, without altering whole body or epididymal fat pad mass.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C78 are supported by data in Figure 4L and Figure 4—figure supplement 1M-Q. The dose-response relationship strengthens the causal inference. The lack of effect on body mass and fat pad mass is important as it rules out indirect effects via weight loss.

results.result: Provision of exogenous CoQ improves insulin-regulated glucose uptake and lower CoQ content may contribute to insulin resistance in adipose tissue and muscle.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C80 are inferences based on the collective data from C63-C78 showing improvements in insulin sensitivity with CoQ supplementation across multiple models and measures. The inference is reasonable and well-supported by the data, though causality is not definitively established.

results.result: 4-nitrobenzoic acid (NB) and 4-chlorobenzoic acid (CB) competitively inhibit Coq2, decreasing mitochondrial CoQ9 to levels similar to insulin-resistant adipocytes. Both inhibitors caused insulin resistance which could be reversed with CoQ provision.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C84 are supported by data in Figure 5A-C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B, with citations to Alam et al., 1975 and Forsman et al., 2010 for the mechanism of action. This is a key experiment establishing sufficiency of CoQ depletion to cause insulin resistance. The reversibility with CoQ supplementation strengthens the causal inference.

results.result: siRNA knockdown of Coq7 or Coq9 lowered mitochondrial CoQ9 and triggered insulin resistance.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C86 are supported by data in Figure 5D-F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-E. This genetic approach complements the pharmacological inhibition and further establishes sufficiency of CoQ depletion to cause insulin resistance. The use of multiple siRNAs (pooled) is appropriate.

results.result: Insulin resistance triggered by pharmacological or genetic inhibition of CoQ biosynthesis occurred independently of consistent defects in insulin signaling to Akt or TBC1D4, or changes in GLUT4 expression. CoQ provision did not alter signaling responses or GLUT4 expression despite improving insulin action, consistent with previous reports that insulin resistance is not driven by overt defects in proximal insulin signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C89 are supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F-Q. C90 is supported by citations to Hoehn et al., 2008 and Tan et al., 2015. This is an important finding indicating that CoQ-mediated insulin resistance acts downstream of or parallel to proximal insulin signaling. The lack of consistent signaling defects is clearly documented.

results.result: Statins have been associated with progression to type 2 diabetes in humans. Both simvastatin and atorvastatin lowered cellular cholesterol and CoQ content in 3T3-L1 adipocytes, induced insulin resistance, and this was reversed by providing CoQ9 or mevalonate, providing evidence that loss of CoQ is sufficient to induce adipocyte insulin resistance and may contribute to off-target effects of statin therapy.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C96 are supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1R-T and citations to Cederberg et al., 2015, Preiss et al., 2011, and Sattar et al., 2010. C97 is an inference that is well-supported by the multiple lines of evidence (pharmacological, genetic, statins). C98 is speculation about clinical implications that is reasonable but not directly tested. The statin experiments provide proof-of-principle that mevalonate pathway inhibition affects CoQ and insulin sensitivity.

results.result: Mitochondrial CoQ is essential for cellular respiration, shuttling electrons from dehydrogenase complexes to complex III, and can regulate superoxide formation from complexes I, II, and III. Excess mitochondrial CoQ can be thought of as an 'electron sink', and previous studies have shown that modest loss of mitochondrial CoQ can be tolerated for electron transport but at the cost of increased mitochondrial oxidants.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C100 are established biochemical knowledge about CoQ function. C101 is a conceptual interpretation that is reasonable. C102 is supported by citation to Quinzii et al., 2008. This provides important background for interpreting the mechanistic studies.

results.result: Total PRDX1-3 content and the dimer:monomer ratio of cytosolic PRDX1 and PRDX2 remained unchanged in insulin-resistant models, but the dimer:monomer ratio of mitochondrial PRDX3 increased significantly in all in vitro models and under conditions of pharmacological or genetic inhibition of CoQ biosynthesis. Restoration of mitochondrial CoQ9 by exogenous provision lowered the PRDX3 dimer:monomer ratio. PRDX3 dimerization was enhanced in insulin-resistant adipose tissue at 5 and 14 day HFHSD feeding, and in vivo CoQ10 administration lowered the PRDX3 dimer-to-monomer ratio dose-dependently, placing decreased mitochondrial CoQ upstream of increased mitochondrial H2O2.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C110 are supported by data in Figure 6A-G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-K. The use of PRDX3 dimerization as a marker of mitochondrial H2O2 is well-established (Bayer et al., 2013). C111 is an inference that is well-supported by the data showing consistent relationship between CoQ levels and PRDX3 dimerization across multiple models and interventions. The compartment-specific effect (mitochondrial PRDX3 but not cytosolic PRDX1/2) is clearly demonstrated.

results.result: Basal oxygen consumption was increased in multiple insulin resistance models in 3T3-L1 adipocytes cultured in galactose. In digitonin-permeabilized adipocytes, FAD-linked respiratory capacity assessed via succinate was the only activity compromised in all models, and this defect was specific to succinate dehydrogenase since oxidation of medium-chain fatty acid was not altered, suggesting that loss of mitochondrial CoQ decreases succinate-driven complex II capacity but does not limit overall mitochondrial respiration.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C114 are supported by oxygen consumption data in Figure 7A-D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, with citation to Ruzicka and Beinert, 1977 for the mechanism of octanoylcarnitine oxidation. C115 is an inference that is reasonable given the data. The finding that overall respiration is not impaired despite complex II defect is important for understanding the mechanism.

results.result: Mitochondrial superoxide was increased in the chronic insulin model and in adipocytes where CoQ biosynthesis was inhibited, as measured by LC-MS quantification of mito-2-hydroxyethidium, implying that increased mitochondrial H2O2 following loss of CoQ was due to increased superoxide production.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C117 are supported by superoxide measurement data in Figure 7E-F, with citation to Zielonka et al., 2008 for the method. C118 is an inference that is reasonable given that superoxide is the precursor of H2O2. The use of a specific LC-MS method for superoxide detection is a strength.

results.result: Uncouplers BAM15 and FCCP lowered PRDX3 dimer/monomer status to control levels in cells with inhibited CoQ biosynthesis, establishing that loss of CoQ increased H2O2 in a coupled respiration-dependent manner. Complex II inhibitors TTFA and malonate lowered PRDX3 dimer/monomer ratio in cells treated to inhibit CoQ biosynthesis and in other insulin resistance models, suggesting that increased H2O2 was dependent on complex II.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C121 are supported by data in Figure 7G-H and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C-E. C120 and C122 are inferences that are reasonable given the effects of uncouplers and complex II inhibitors. The use of multiple inhibitors (TTFA, malonate) and uncouplers (BAM15, FCCP) strengthens the conclusions.

results.result: Rotenone had no effect on PRDX3 redox state in NB-treated cells, and treatment with NB did not change CoQ redox state. Since a more reduced CoQ pool is required for reverse electron transport, these data suggest that reverse electron transport was not involved in the observed increase in superoxide/H2O2, and that complex II itself was the likely origin of the oxidants.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C124 are supported by data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F-G. C125-C126 are inferences supported by citations to Murphy, 2009 and Quinlan et al., 2012. The logic is sound: lack of rotenone effect and unchanged CoQ redox state argue against reverse electron transport, pointing to complex II as the source. This is a key mechanistic finding.

results.result: Treatment of control adipocytes with TTFA did not impair insulin-stimulated HA-GLUT4 translocation, suggesting that impaired complex II activity does not cause insulin resistance per se. However, both TTFA and malonate improved insulin-stimulated HA-GLUT4 translocation in all insulin resistance models tested, and TTFA improved insulin-stimulated 2DOG uptake in adipose explants from HFHSD-fed mice, suggesting that lower mitochondrial CoQ accelerates superoxide generation from complex II, elevating mitochondrial H2O2 burden and driving insulin resistance.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C130 are supported by data in Figure 7I-K. C128 and C131 are inferences that are reasonable given the data. The finding that complex II inhibition improves insulin sensitivity in insulin-resistant but not control cells is important for understanding the mechanism. C131 represents a synthesis of the mechanistic findings.

results.result: Mitochondrial oxidants have been reported to play an important role in the development of insulin resistance in adipose and muscle tissue, thought to occur primarily via increased production of superoxide or H2O2 in mitochondria, yet the proximal mechanism triggering mitochondrial oxidant production has remained elusive.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C133 are supported by citations to Hoehn et al., 2009, Houstis et al., 2006, Paglialunga et al., 2015, and Anderson et al., 2009. This provides important context for the significance of the current findings.

results.result: Mass-spectrometry-based proteomic analysis revealed down-regulation of the mevalonate/CoQ biosynthesis pathway in multiple models, and targeted metabolite analysis revealed a common decrease in mitochondrial CoQ content in insulin-resistant adipose tissue, 3T3-L1 adipocytes, and muscle. Decreased mitochondrial CoQ was sufficient to cause insulin resistance via a mechanism requiring mitochondrial oxidants, while restoration of mitochondrial CoQ restored insulin sensitivity. The pathway involves decreased expression of mevalonate pathway/CoQ biosynthetic enzymes, lower mitochondrial CoQ, and insulin resistance as a result of oxidant production primarily from complex II.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C137 are supported by the collective proteomic and metabolite data throughout the manuscript. C138 is a summary of the main findings that accurately represents the data. This represents the core conclusion of the study integrating multiple lines of evidence.

results.result: Many insults implicated in insulin resistance including hyperinsulinemia, inflammation, corticosteroids, and caloric excess converge upon loss of mitochondrial CoQ as a potential cause of insulin resistance, which could be explained by decreased expression of CoQ biosynthetic enzymes and lower CoQ synthesis rates in a majority of models studied.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C140 are inferences based on the observation that multiple different models all exhibit decreased mitochondrial CoQ and decreased expression/synthesis of CoQ biosynthetic components. The inference is reasonable and represents an important conceptual advance, though the mechanisms by which different insults affect CoQ biosynthesis may differ.

results.result: The finding that mevalonate pathway inhibiting statins lowered CoQ content and caused insulin resistance in a CoQ-dependent manner may shed new light on the link between statin therapy in humans and insulin resistance.
results.evaluation: Claim C141 is speculation about clinical implications based on the statin experiments and citations to Cederberg et al., 2015, Preiss et al., 2011, and Sattar et al., 2010. The speculation is reasonable given the data but represents hypothesis generation rather than direct evidence. The statin experiments were conducted in vitro, so extrapolation to human statin therapy requires caution.

results.result: The lack of concordance between transcript and protein expression within the mevalonate/CoQ pathway across different insulin-resistant models suggests multiple mechanisms may target this pathway in response to different upstream insults, mediated via transcriptional or post-translational regulation. Subcellular analysis of CoQ content and data from the chronic insulin model indicate that other aspects of CoQ biology may be involved in regulating mitochondrial CoQ abundance in insulin-resistant conditions, supporting the notion that various insults act in different ways, all decreasing mitochondrial CoQ as a common means of inducing insulin resistance.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C144 are inferences based on the observed lack of concordance between transcript and protein expression and the paradoxical findings in the chronic insulin model. The inferences are reasonable and acknowledge the complexity of CoQ regulation. C143 is speculation that is appropriately qualified.

results.result: Modest loss of CoQ has been reported to increase mitochondrial oxidants in various cellular systems. The authors hypothesize that increased superoxide production from the IIF site is due to increased steady-state concentrations of the flavin radical as a result of impaired electron transfer to CoQ at the IIQ binding site, supported by the finding that maximal complex II activity was impaired in all models. Alternatively, lower CoQ may favor reverse electron transfer to complex II under conditions where other enzymes are feeding electrons into the CoQ pool. There are likely additional sites of superoxide production since complex II inhibition only partially rescued PRDX3 dimerization.
results.evaluation: Claim C145 is supported by citations to Cornelius et al., 2013, Duberley et al., 2013, Quinzii et al., 2013, Quinzii et al., 2012, and Rodríguez-Hernández et al., 2009. C146 is a hypothesis that is reasonable given the observed decrease in complex II activity. C147 is supported by the oxygen consumption data. C148 is speculation about an alternative mechanism supported by citations to Orr et al., 2012 and Quinlan et al., 2012. C149 is an inference based on the partial rescue by complex II inhibitors. The mechanistic discussion is appropriately speculative while being grounded in the data.

results.result: Improvements in insulin-stimulated glucose transport and inhibition of lipolysis with CoQ supplementation were not associated with improved insulin signaling to Akt or TBC1D4, consistent with previous reports that defects in insulin-stimulated glucose transport are not due to obvious defects in proximal insulin signaling. It seems unlikely that mitochondrial oxidant-induced insulin resistance requires changes in transcription because induction of mitochondrial oxidants acutely impairs insulin action, suggesting a presently undiscovered signal transduction pathway that communicates directly to mediators of insulin action in the cytoplasm.
results.evaluation: Claim C150 is supported by insulin signaling data. C151 is supported by citations to Hoehn et al., 2008 and Tan et al., 2015. C152 is an inference supported by citation to Hoehn et al., 2009. C153 is speculation about a potential mechanism. The discussion appropriately acknowledges the gap in understanding of how mitochondrial oxidants affect insulin action.

results.result: Serum and tissue CoQ10 concentrations are decreased in individuals with diabetes and cardiovascular disease. While there are reports of CoQ supplementation benefiting these conditions, the efficacy of CoQ10 in treatment remains unclear. This study provides a reasonable rationale for targeting the CoQ biosynthesis pathway as a potential therapeutic target.
results.evaluation: Claims C154-C156 are supported by citations to multiple studies. C157 is an inference based on the findings that is reasonable. This provides context for the therapeutic implications of the work.

results.result: Overall low bioavailability of orally administered CoQ10 represents a substantial limitation. Intra-peritoneal administration of CoQ to mice provided proof-of-principle that restoration of mitochondrial CoQ improves insulin action and glucose tolerance, but this is not likely a practical strategy for humans. Pharmacological approaches targeting the CoQ biosynthesis pathway or additional processes regulating mitochondrial CoQ content may represent potential options in the future.
results.evaluation: Claim C158 is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 1995. C159 is supported by data in Figure 4. C160 is a logical inference about practicality. C161 is speculation about potential therapeutic strategies supported by citation to Bentinger et al., 2008. The discussion of therapeutic implications is appropriately cautious.

results.result: The protein levels, but not mRNA levels, of COQ7 and COQ9 were decreased in insulin resistance. These proteins form a dimeric complex that may be regulated via post-translational mechanisms. The CoQ biosynthetic protein complex has been reported to be stabilized by ADCK3/COQ8, mitochondrial proteases, and CoQ itself. Destabilization of the complex lowers expression of COQ3, 7, and 9, suggesting that loss of COQ7 and 9 in insulin resistance may result from increased turnover due to complex instability.
results.evaluation: Claim C162 is supported by proteomic and transcriptomic data. C163 is supported by citation to Lohman et al., 2014. C164-C166 are supported by citations to He et al., 2014, Stefely et al., 2016, and Veling et al., 2017. C167 is established knowledge. C168 is speculation that is reasonable given the known mechanisms of COQ protein complex regulation.

results.result: Recent chemical screens have successfully identified compounds that prevent superoxide production from complex I and III without impairing electron transport. Identifying similar compounds for complex II may be useful in mitigating superoxide/H2O2 production and overcoming insulin resistance.
results.evaluation: Claims C169-C170 are supported by citations to Brand et al., 2016 and Orr et al., 2015. C171 is speculation about a potential therapeutic strategy that is reasonable given the findings implicating complex II as the source of oxidants.

results.result: Over-expression of mitochondria-targeted catalase lowered the PRDX3 dimer:monomer ratio and improved insulin responses in cells where CoQ biosynthesis was inhibited, consistent with loss of mitochondrial CoQ causing insulin resistance via mitochondrial H2O2.
results.evaluation: Claims C172-C173 are supported by data in Figure 6H-J and Figure 6—figure supplement 1M-O. C174 is an inference that is well-supported by the data. The catalase overexpression experiment provides strong evidence for the role of mitochondrial H2O2 in mediating the effects of CoQ depletion on insulin sensitivity.
